title: Taylor and Maclaurin Series
lead: If a function has a power series, its coefficients are fixed by its derivatives at the center. This section builds the Taylor series and Taylor polynomials from those derivatives, bounds the error of a polynomial approximation with Taylor’s theorem with remainder, and asks when the series converges to the function.
objectives: Describe the procedure for finding a Taylor polynomial of a given order for a function.
Explain the meaning and significance of Taylor’s theorem with remainder.
Estimate the remainder for a Taylor series approximation of a given function.
summary_html:
• Taylor polynomials are used to approximate functions near a value $x=a.$ Maclaurin polynomials are Taylor polynomials at $x=0.$
  • The nth degree Taylor polynomials for a function $f$ are the partial sums of the Taylor series for $f.$
  • If a function $f$ has a power series representation at $x=a,$ then it is given by its Taylor series at $x=a.$
  • A Taylor series for $f$ converges to $f$ if and only if $\lim_{n\to \infty}\kR_{n}(x)=0$ where $\kR_{n}(x)=\kf(x)-\kp_{n}(x).$
  • The Taylor series for ex, $\sin x,$ and $\cos x$ converge to the respective functions for all real x.
notes: The media note linking to the MacTutor History of Mathematics biographies of Brook Taylor and Colin Maclaurin is left out.

exercises.prompt: Find the Taylor polynomials $p_{0},p_{1},p_{2}$ and $p_{3}$ for $f(x)=\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ at $x=1.$

answer.hint: Find the first three derivatives of $f$ and evaluate them at $x=1.$

exercises.prompt: Find formulas for the Maclaurin polynomials $p_{0},p_{1},p_{2}$ and $p_{3}$ for $f(x)=\frac{1}{1+x}.$ Find a formula for the nth Maclaurin polynomial. Write your answer using sigma notation.

answer.hint: Evaluate the first four derivatives of $f$ and look for a pattern.

exercises.prompt: Find the first and second Taylor polynomials for $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ at $x=4.$ Use these polynomials to estimate $\sqrt{6}.$ Use Taylor’s theorem to bound the error.
Use the fourth Maclaurin polynomial for $\cos x$ to approximate $\cos (\frac{\pi}{12}).$
Find the Taylor series for $f(x)=\frac{1}{2x}$ at $x=2$ and determine its interval of convergence.

answer.solution: $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{{(2-x)}^{n}}{2^{n+1}}.$<sup class="fn" data-note="c-cp1014-series"></sup> The interval of convergence is $(0,4).$

exercises.prompt: Find the Maclaurin series for $f(x)=\cos x.$ Use the ratio test to show that the interval of convergence is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ Show that the Maclaurin series converges to $\cos x$ for all real numbers x.

answer.solution: $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{{(-1)}^{n}x^{2n}}{(2n)!}$ By the ratio test, the interval of convergence is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ Since $|R_{n}(x)|\le \frac{{|x|}^{n+1}}{(n+1)!},$ the series converges to $\cos x$ for all real x.
answer.hint: Use the Maclaurin polynomials for $\cos x.$

[T] ${(28)}^{1/3};a=27,n=1$

answer.solution: $\frac{d^{2}}{dx^{2}}x^{1/3}=-\frac{2}{9x^{5/3}}\ge -0.00092\text{…}$ when $x\ge 28$ so the remainder estimate applies to the linear approximation $x^{1/3}\approx p_{1}(27)=3+\frac{x-27}{27},$ which gives ${(28)}^{1/3}\approx 3+\frac{1}{27}=3.\overline{037},$ while ${(28)}^{1/3}\approx 3.03658.$

answer.solution: Since $\frac{d^{n}}{dx^{n}}(\ln x)={(-1)}^{n-1}\frac{(n-1)!}{x^{n}},R_{1000}\approx \frac{1}{1001}.$ One has $p_{1000}(1)=\sum_{n=1}^{1000} \frac{{(-1)}^{n-1}}{n} \approx 0.6936$<sup class="fn" data-note="c-e129-sum"></sup> whereas $\ln (2)\approx 0.6931\cdots .$

In the following exercises, find the smallest value of n such that the remainder estimate $|R_{n}|\le \frac{M}{(n+1)!}{(x-a)}^{n+1},$ where M is the maximum value of $|f^{(n+1)}(z)|$ on the interval between a and the indicated point, yields $|R_{n}|\le \frac{1}{1000}$ on the indicated interval.

$f(x)=\cos x$ on $[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}],a=0$

answer.solution: Since $f^{(n+1)}(z)$ is $\sin z$ or $\cos z,$ we have $M=1.$ Since $|x-0|\le \frac{\pi}{2},$ we seek the smallest n such that $\frac{{\pi}^{n+1}}{2^{n+1}(n+1)!}\le 0.001.$ The smallest such value is $n=7.$ The remainder estimate is $R_{7}\le 0.00092.$

$f(x)=e^{-x}$ on $[-3,3],a=0$

answer.solution: Since $f^{(n+1)}(z)=\text{±}e^{-z}$ one has $M=e^{3}.$ Since $|x-0|\le 3,$ one seeks the smallest n such that $\frac{3^{n+1}e^{3}}{(n+1)!}\le 0.001.$ The smallest such value is $n=14.$ The remainder estimate is $R_{14}\le 0.000220.$

footnotes.html: The index here is $m$: the formula that follows holds for $m\ge 0.$

The numerator is printed as 0.0011468; it is $f^{\prime\prime\prime}(8)\approx 0.0014468,$ found just above, and the bound 0.0065104 is computed from that value: $\frac{0.0014468}{3!}\cdot 27\approx 0.0065104.$
The remainder formula comes from Taylor’s Theorem with Remainder, not from Uniqueness of Taylor Series.

For $f(x)=\frac{1}{2x}=\frac{1}{2}x^{-1},$ the derivatives are $f^{(n)}(2)=\frac{{(-1)}^{n}n!}{2\cdot 2^{n+1}}=\frac{{(-1)}^{n}n!}{2^{n+2}},$ and the Taylor series is $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{{(2-x)}^{n}}{2^{n+2}};$ the hint and the answer print $2^{n+1}.$ At $x=2$ the printed series gives $\frac{1}{2},$ not $f(2)=\frac{1}{4}.$ The interval of convergence, $(0,4),$ is right.

The partial sum is $p_{1000}(2),$ the polynomial at $x=2$ ($p_{1000}(1)=0$), and $\sum_{n=1}^{1000}\frac{{(-1)}^{n-1}}{n}\approx 0.69265,$ below $\ln 2$ by about $\frac{1}{2000},$ within the estimate $R_{1000}\approx\frac{1}{1001}.$
The largest value of $|\cos z|$ on $[-R,R]$ is 1, at $z=0,$ so the condition is $\frac{R^{2}}{2}\le 0.1,$ that is $R^{2}\le 0.2$ and $R\le \sqrt{0.2}\approx 0.447,$ the value given.
The series is that of $-\sin (x-\frac{\pi}{2});$ $-\cos (x-\frac{\pi}{2})$ is printed.

derivations.what: the convergence of a Taylor series
derivations.source: Calculus, 10.3 Taylor and Maclaurin Series, Convergence of Taylor Series

assumes.text: A series converges to a value exactly when its sequence of partial sums converges to that value.
The $n$th partial sum of the Taylor series for $f$ at $a$ is the $n$th Taylor polynomial $\kp_{n}(x).$
The limit of a difference is the difference of the limits.

steps.cap: $\kf(x)$ does not depend on $n,$ so the limit is $\kf(x)$ less the limit of $\kR_{n}(x).$

derivations.what: the Maclaurin series for $e^{x}$ converging to $e^{x}$
derivations.source: Calculus, 10.3 Taylor and Maclaurin Series, Example 10.16

assumes.text: If $\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{|a_{n+1}|}{|a_{n}|}\lt 1,$ then $\sum a_{n}$ converges absolutely.

then.why: The terms of the Maclaurin series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n}}{n!}$ are $a_{n}=\frac{x^{n}}{n!}.$

assumes.text: For each $x$ there is a $c$ between $0$ and $x$ with $\kR_{n}(x)=\frac{\kfnplusone(c)}{(n+1)!}x^{n+1};$ if $|\kfnplusone|\le M$ there, then $|\kR_{n}(x)|\le \frac{M}{(n+1)!}{|x|}^{n+1}.$
$e^{x}$ is increasing, so its largest value for $|x|\le b$ is $e^{b}.$
If $\sum a_{n}$ converges, then $\lim_{n\to \infty}a_{n}=0.$
A sequence held between $0$ and a sequence with limit $0$ has limit $0.$
The Taylor series converges to $\kf(x)$ exactly when $\lim_{n\to \infty}\kR_{n}(x)=0.$

steps.cap: The bound is $e^{b}$ times a sequence with limit $0,$ so it has limit $0.$
